target: Let L be the logarithms of nonzero algebraic numbers. (A) Diaz's (Qr2) in transcendence degree one: if l0, l1 in L are neither real nor purely imaginary, the field Q(l0, l1, conj l0, conj l1) has transcendence degree at most 1, and l1/l0 is real or purely imaginary, then l1/l0 is rational. (B) Pair rigidity: if u, v in L are nonzero, |u|^2/|v|^2 is rational and Q(u, v, conj u, conj v) has transcendence degree at most 1, then v is in Qu or in Q conj u. The target is a printed statement of (A) or (B), or a printed result that yields them, other than Brownawell's Corollaries 5 and 7 and the four exponentials theorem in transcendence degree one.

leads.citation: D. Roy, M. Waldschmidt, Approximation diophantienne et indépendance algébrique de logarithmes, Ann. Sci. ENS (4) 30 (1997), 753-796
leads.derivation: My translation; the paper does not state (A) or (B). Theorem 0.2: a point with coordinates in L on a zero set of a homogeneous rational P of degree at most 2 lies in a rational subspace U contained in V, unless the field has transcendence degree at least 2. (B): take P = X1X2 - cX3X4 with c = |u|^2/|v|^2 at (u, conj u, v, conj v). The coordinate forms on U satisfy f1f2 = c f3f4 in a polynomial ring over Q, so unique factorisation gives f1 proportional to f3 or f4 over Q, that is v in Qu or v in Q conj u. (A): take P = X1X4 - X2X3 (real ratio) or X1X4 + X2X3 (imaginary ratio) at (l1, conj l1, l0, conj l0). Then f1 is proportional to f2 or f3. l1 = r conj l1 forces r = ±1, which the hypothesis excludes, so l1 is in Ql0. L is stable under conjugation. Conceptually this is no stronger for the target than Brownawell's Corollary 7, of which the case P = X1X4 - X2X3 is the equivalent form.

leads.citation: M. Waldschmidt, Diophantine Approximation on Linear Algebraic Groups, Grundlehren 326, Springer, 2000
leads.quote: for any nonzero homogeneous polynomial Q of degree 2
leads.derivation: My translation; the book does not state (A) or (B). Take a Q-basis λ of the Q-span of (u, conj u, v, conj v). Basis elements lie in L, and the transcendence degree is exactly 1 by Hermite-Lindemann. The rational polynomial f1f2 - c f3f4 in the λ vanishes at λ, so it is the zero polynomial; factorising as for Roy-Waldschmidt gives (B), and the same substitution with X1X4 ∓ X2X3 gives (A).

leads.citation: D. Roy, M. Waldschmidt, Quadratic relations between logarithms of algebraic numbers, Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A 71 (1995), 151-153
leads.location: Theorem 2, p. 151 (announcement; proof given in the 1997 paper)
leads.quote: contained in a vector subspace of C^n which is defined over Q
leads.derivation: Earlier announcement of the same statement as Théorème 0.2 of the 1997 paper, for transcendence degree 1, so the same translation applies. The text layer is garbled and the two-column layout is scrambled; I did not check this page against the image, though the 1997 statement was checked.

leads.citation: D. Roy, M. Waldschmidt, Approximation diophantienne et indépendance algébrique de logarithmes, Ann. Sci. ENS (4) 30 (1997), 753-796
leads.quote: λ et son conjugué complexe λ̄ soient algébriquement dépendants sur Q
leads.derivation: These are the closest printed statements in form: a logarithm and its complex conjugate in transcendence degree one, via Théorème 0.2. Their conclusion is transcendence of exp(sqrt(q(λ, conj λ))), for example exp(|λ|). They do not concern a second logarithm or the ratio, and so do not yield (A) or (B); only the parent Théorème 0.2 does.

leads.citation: G. Diaz, Produits et quotients de combinaisons linéaires de logarithmes de nombres algébriques, J. Théor. Nombres Bordeaux 19 (2007), 373-391
leads.location: Remarque after Théorème 4 and Corollaire 6(2), pp. 386-387
leads.quote: degré de transcendance sur Q inférieur ou égal à 1
leads.derivation: Diaz prints the Brownawell-Waldschmidt four-logarithm form on p. 386, then returns to (Qr). His partial result, Corollaire 6(2), proves (Qr2) under the different hypothesis that l1/l0 lies in the Q-bar span of 1 and L. He does not make the transcendence-degree-one substitution; his only illustration of the remark is the l^2, l^3 corollary. This confirms the paper does not contain the target, and the input is already named in the target.

notes:
**Outcome.** I found no printed statement of (A) or (B). The "not found" stands for a literal statement. It is not broken in the sense of a source saying this; the one new item is a more general printed theorem than the target names.

**Best lead.** Roy-Waldschmidt 1997, Théorème 0.2 (announced in 1995, Theorem 2), restated in DALAG p. 593. The target names only the four exponentials theorem and Brownawell. These sources print the general homogeneous-quadratic version, so both (A) and (B) come from one printed theorem with a single choice of P. The translation is mine:
- (B): P = X1X2 - cX3X4 at (u, conj u, v, conj v).
- (A): P = X1X4 ∓ X2X3 at (l1, conj l1, l0, conj l0).

Then use unique factorisation of the linear forms on the rational subspace. I checked Théorème 0.2 on the page image: P has rational coefficients, and Conjecture 0.3 on the same page uses Q-bar, so the bold Q is rational. That is enough for rational c and ±1. This does not add depth over Brownawell's Corollary 7, because the case P = X1X4 - X2X3 is equivalent to it. It is a second printed route, not an earlier statement of the target.

**Nearest in form.** RW97 Corollaires 7.3 and 7.4 use λ and conj λ algebraically dependent, with q(λ, conj λ) under exp. They show the authors had the conjugation-in-transcendence-degree-one idea in print, but the conclusions concern exp(sqrt(q)), not a second logarithm. Analogue only. The paper's own example is exp(sqrt((log 2)^2 + π^2)). The proofs rest on the same Théorème 0.2.

**Diaz 2007.** Pages 386-387 print the Brownawell-Waldschmidt theorem right next to (Qr), but the only illustration is the l^2, l^3 corollary, and Corollaire 6 uses Théorème 4 instead. Diaz's proof that (C4E) implies (Qr2) uses families (1, l1/l0) and (l0, conj l0) on p. 377. Combining that with the p. 386 theorem gives (A) in two lines, yet he does not write it. That supports the "routine" class.

**Waldschmidt's conjugation survey and Variations.** Neither has a transcendence-degree-one statement with conjugates. Their conjugation results rest on the six exponentials theorems.

**Forward citations.** Semantic Scholar lists one citer of Diaz 2007 (Waldschmidt's 2005 survey), and OpenAlex shows 0. No citer of Diaz 2007 after 2007 appeared in any index I could open. Citers of Brownawell 1974 and Roy-Waldschmidt are about approximation or independence criteria by title. The ones I screened after August 2026 look irrelevant from their titles.

**Coverage after 5 October 2026 is weak.** arXiv API and OpenAlex lists were rate limited, zbMATH citing queries failed, and Crossref keyword searches were noisy. I found nothing, but this is not a complete check. I excluded the carlok repository and prove2.me pages that surfaced in search and used nothing from them.

**Not settled.**
- The zbMATH list of citers of Diaz 2007.
- The arXiv math.NT listing for October-November 2026.
- Lecture notes and books that I saw only partly, such as Chap. 13 of Nesterenko-Philippon.

I stopped after about 7 minutes of wall clock (15:54 to about 16:01), well inside the time box, because further citation chains were blocked by rate limits and the remaining citers looked off-topic by title. A re-run of the blocked indexes could close the gaps.
